name: Tropical rainforest
notes: Ever-wet lowland rainforest: multi-layered evergreen broadleaf forest with buttressed canopy, giant emergents, palms, lianas and heavy epiphyte load. Drawn on the Amazon, Congo Basin and Sundaland (Borneo/Malaya) dipterocarp forest.

emergent.name: Brazil nut tree
emergent.source: Bertholletia excelsa, Brazil nut, emergent of non-flooded Amazon terra firme forest, 30-50 m — Wikipedia / Kew

traits.native_range: Bertholletia excelsa, Brazil nut, emergent of non-flooded Amazon terra firme forest, 30-50 m — Wikipedia / Kew

emergent.silhouette: tall straight bole with small round crown above canopy

growth.juvenile_note: The big woody seed germinates slowly: often 12-18 months after an agouti buries it (1-3 months if the shell is removed). A shoot with small scale leaves comes first, then true leaves. The sapling is a straight, slender whip with large, leathery, oblong, wavy-edged leaves; in shade it can wait for years almost dormant, then rockets up when a treefall opens a gap.
growth.source: Wikipedia (to 50 m, lives 500 to ~1000 yr, saplings wait years in shade for a gap); Brazil-nut agronomy and extractive-reserve studies (intact seeds germinate after 12-18 months, 1-3 months without testa; plantation seedlings fruit from ~10-15 yr, grafts ~8 yr); height-growth timings estimated.

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (cream 6-petalled flowers with a hood-shaped stamen mass, one-day flowers pollinated only by large bees: Bombus, Centris, Epicharis, Eulaema, Xylocopa; capsule 10-15 cm, up to 2 kg, 8-24 seeds, 14 months from pollination to ripe; agoutis open fallen fruit); fruit set and crop from harvest studies, approximate.

emergent.name: Kapok
emergent.source: Ceiba pentandra, kapok, buttressed emergent of neotropical and West African rainforest, up to 70 m — Wikipedia

traits.native_range: Ceiba pentandra, kapok, buttressed emergent of neotropical and West African rainforest, up to 70 m — Wikipedia

emergent.silhouette: giant buttressed trunk, flat tiered crown above canopy

growth.juvenile_note: Epigeal seedling with two broad leafy cotyledons; the first leaves are small with few leaflets, soon palmate with 5-9 leaflets. The sapling has a smooth GREEN trunk studded with stout conical thorns and grows straight and fast, with horizontal branches in widely spaced whorls, giving a tiered pagoda-like cone before it later spreads into a flat emergent crown on huge buttresses.
growth.source: ICRAF Agroforestree Ceiba pentandra (white to rose petals, flowers open soon after dark, fruit bats, hawkmoths and bees; capsule 10-30 cm, 120-175 seeds); Wikipedia (to 60 m, 5-9 leaflets, several hundred pods per tree); growth, first flowering and lifespan estimated from PROSEA-style kapok data

fruiting.source: ICRAF Agroforestree Ceiba pentandra (flowers in dry season on leafless branches, open at dusk for one night, bats then moths and bees; capsules 10-30 cm split along 5 lines releasing kapok floss and 120-175 seeds); Wikipedia (several hundred pods per tree)

canopy.name: Moriche palm

growth.juvenile_note: The seed sends a germination tube down into the wet soil from which the seedling rises. The first leaves are simple, strap-like pleated blades; later leaves turn into huge rounded costapalmate fans on long stalks. For years it is a stemless tuft of fans in the swamp while the trunk base thickens underground, then a smooth grey column rises and old leaves fall cleanly away.
growth.source: Wikipedia Mauritia flexuosa (to 35 m, flowers Dec-Apr, scaly chestnut fruit with yellow pulp, seeds float and are spread by floods and fish); palm establishment and growth rates estimated from Mauritia/Neotropical fan-palm literature

canopy.source: Palm of Amazon and Orinoco swamps; height 20-35 m. Fan palm of the swamps; buriti. Standard floras and Kew POWO for the name.

canopy.name: Rubber tree
canopy.source: Hevea brasiliensis, para rubber tree, scattered canopy tree of Amazonian terra firme and seasonally flooded forest, 20-40 m in the wild (Kew POWO: native to N South America; Schultes 1970; Webster & Paardekooper 1989 Rubber)

bark.notes: smooth pale grey-brown bark; cut bark bleeds white latex

flower.form: small bell-shaped creamy-yellow flowers in loose panicles, strongly scented

fruit.form: three-lobed capsule 3-5 cm that bursts with a crack, flinging mottled seeds

appearance.seasonal: brief leaf change (wintering) in the drier months: old leaves turn orange-red and fall, new flush follows within weeks
appearance.silhouette: tall straight grey bole, open crown of three-leaflet tiers
appearance.refs: Kew POWO Hevea brasiliensis; Wikipedia; Webster & Paardekooper 1989

growth.juvenile_note: Seed germinates within 1-3 weeks (it loses viability fast); the cotyledons stay in the seed. The seedling grows in rhythmic flushes: a length of bare stem, then a storey of long-stalked three-leaflet leaves, then a pause, so the sapling is a thin straight whip with tiers of leaves along it. Branches begin at a few metres; wild trees keep a straight, clean bole.
growth.source: Webster & Paardekooper 1989 Rubber (flushing growth, first flowering at 4-5 yr, seed viability of weeks); Wikipedia Hevea brasiliensis (wild trees to 43 m, lifespan over 100 yr). Height curve and lifespan of wild trees estimated.

fruiting.source: Webster & Paardekooper 1989 (monoecious panicles of many male and few female flowers at leaf flush; midge and thrips pollination; natural fruit set ~3-5 %; three-seeded capsule ripens in ~5 months and splits explosively, seeds thrown up to 15 m; raw seed cyanogenic). Crop per tree estimated.

canopy.name: Walking palm

growth.juvenile_note: The first leaves are bifid (two-lobed) eophylls on a stemless seedling. The young palm soon lifts itself on a cone of spiny stilt roots, adding new stilts on the side toward light while older ones rot, and a slim grey trunk rises with a pale green-blue crownshaft and a few spreading pinnate leaves with jagged, split leaflets.
growth.source: Henderson, Galeano & Bernal 1995 Field Guide to the Palms of the Americas (stems to 20(-30) m, stilt-root cone to 2 m, leaflets split longitudinally, praemorse); Bodley & Benson 1980 on the 'walking' myth. First fruiting and lifespan estimated.

canopy.source: Palm of Amazon and Central American rainforest; height 15-25 m. Stilt roots; the tripod palm. Standard floras and Kew POWO for the name.
canopy.silhouette: slim grey palm perched on a cone of spiny stilt roots

fruiting.source: Henderson et al. 1995 (inflorescences below the crownshaft, cream flowers, beetle-pollinated; ellipsoid fruit 2-3.5 cm, yellowish-brown when ripe, eaten by mammals and birds). Phenology and counts estimated.

canopy.silhouette: spiny climbing cane trailing through canopy

growth.juvenile_note: Seeds sprout in 1-2 months; the first leaf is a bifid 'fishtail' eophyll, followed by a slowly enlarging rosette of pinnate leaves on very spiny sheaths. After 2-3 years the single stem begins to elongate, and the thick cane climbs by long whip-like leaf tips armed with backward hooks, shedding its lower leaves.
growth.source: Wikipedia (solitary, dioecious, cane to 8 cm thick and over 100 m long, grows 1-3 m a year, up to 7 m/yr in Sabah; fruit to 2.8 x 2 cm with 15 rows of yellowish scales); PROSEA-style rattan culture for germination and rosette stage; first flowering and lifespan estimated.

fruiting.source: Wikipedia (dioecious; fruit rounded to ovoid, to 2.8 x 2 cm, covered in 15 rows of yellowish scales with blackish-brown margins); rattan fruits take ~1 yr to ripen and their sour sarcotesta is eaten; phenology and counts estimated.

shrub.name: Giant taro

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling: one small heart- to arrow-shaped leaf on a thin stalk from a pea-sized corm, then a low rosette of a few glossy green arrowhead leaves on long fleshy stalks. Within 1-2 years a thick, ringed, above-ground stem forms and suckers sprout at its base; leaves grow to 1-2 m, held nearly upright with the tip pointing up.
growth.source: Useful Tropical Plants (Alocasia macrorrhizos: 2-4 m, occasionally 5; stems to 3 m or more and 20 cm thick; 400-600 days to mature; seed germinates best at 24 C; grows best in some shade, tolerates full sun and deep shade; thermogenic spadix, insect-pollinated). Germination days, first flowering and lifespan estimated.

shrub.name: Wild banana

growth.juvenile_note: Seedling: the first leaves are small, narrow and lance-shaped, rolled round one another into a short soft pseudostem. Each new leaf is broader until the plant is a small copy of the adult with a green, often dark-blotched pseudostem. Each pseudostem flowers once and dies; narrow-leaved 'sword suckers' rise from the rhizome to replace it, so the clump lives on for decades.
growth.source: ProMusa and Simmonds 'Bananas' (pseudostem fruits ~1-1.5 yr after emergence and then dies; suckers replace it; seeds of wild bananas germinate slowly and erratically over weeks to months); timings from seed estimated

Each rainy season the young clump sends up stouter culms than the year before, reaching full-size culms (up to ~30 m tall, 20-28 cm thick) after roughly a decade. New shoots are fat conical spears wrapped in large brown hairy sheaths that elongate up to 40 cm a day; culm branches and leaves appear only after the culm reaches full height.

Culm elongation time (~3-4 months), culm lifespan, clump build-up and gregarious flowering interval (reported ~40 yr) estimated from bamboo literature.

growth.source: Estimated from genus Adiantum (A. capillus-veneris spore culture: fernlets in ~2-3 months) and Flora descriptions of A. latifolium (long-creeping rhizome; forms colonies in disturbed tropical American forest and roadsides)

ground.name: Taro

growth.juvenile_note: Almost always grows from a corm or side cormel (true seed is rare): a pointed shoot unrolls into a small rosette of long-stalked leaves. growth.source: Wikipedia Taro (leaves to 40 x 25 cm on 0.8-1.2 m petioles; matures 6-12 months after planting on dry land, 12-15 months in wetland, early cultivars 5-7 months; propagated by corms and cormels; perennial); PROSEA/FAO taro accounts (sprouting in 2-4 weeks, flowering rare, grows in partial shade)

repro.note: giant herbs, not trees: each stem grows in a season, fruits or flowers once and dies, replaced by suckers from the clump — fast growth stages, visible in weeks

The young fern is a small open funnel of undivided glossy fronds with a dark midrib that widens year by year into a nest-like rosette catching leaf litter.

repro.note: spores by wind and water; no flowers; needs a wet film to reproduce, so spread reads moisture not pollinators
